BANK.q: A client asks which medication will lower a fever and relieve a headache but will NOT reduce joint swelling. Which medication fits?
BANK.r: Acetaminophen works only in the CNS: blocks spinal pain pathways and acts on the hypothalamus to reduce fever. It does NOT reduce inflammation.

BANK.q: A client is prescribed long-term naproxen (COX-1 inhibitor). Which adverse effects should the client watch for? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: COX-1 normally protects gastric mucosa, supports platelet aggregation and kidney function. Blocking it → ulcer, bleeding, kidney dysfunction (higher risk with diabetes). HTN/clots/MI/stroke = COX-2.

BANK.q: A client taking celecoxib calls the clinic. Which report needs immediate follow-up?
o: New chest pain and one-sided arm weakness
Dark green stools after taking iron
BANK.r: COX-2 inhibitors increase platelet aggregation and cause vasoconstriction → hypertension, clots, MI, stroke.

BANK.q: A post-op client on IV morphine has RR 7/min and is difficult to arouse. Which medication does the nurse anticipate?
BANK.r: Opioid agonists suppress brainstem respiratory centers. Naloxone is the antagonist: binds the receptor to block/reverse the response.

BANK.q: A client is on long-term glucocorticoids. What belongs in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
o: Stop the medication as soon as it is no longer needed
BANK.r: Effects: immunosuppression, hyperglycemia, muscle wasting, bone demineralization, fluid retention + weight GAIN. Never stop abruptly — taper.

BANK.q: A client abruptly stopped long-term prednisone. Which findings indicate adrenal crisis? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Endogenous production is suppressed → abrupt withdrawal causes adrenal crisis: hypotension, hypoglycemia, fever, confusion, vomiting.

BANK.q: A client with gout starts allopurinol. Which instruction is the priority?
BANK.r: More uric acid excreted by the kidneys → uric acid renal stones. Teach hydration / increase fluids.

BANK.q: Which dinner choice shows a client with gout understands dietary teaching?
BANK.r: Purines → uric acid. High-purine foods: red meat, organ meat, beer, seafood.

BANK.q: Which normal prostaglandin function explains why aspirin can cause a gastric ulcer?
o: Protecting gastric mucosa by stimulating mucus secretion
BANK.r: Prostaglandins protect gastric mucosa by stimulating mucus. COX-1 inhibitors (aspirin) remove that protection.

BANK.q: Which chemical messengers are released by injured cells and stimulate nociceptors? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Injury releases substance P, bradykinins, histamine, prostaglandins → nociceptors → impulse → spinal cord → brain. Endorphins, enkephalins, serotonin are the brain's natural painkillers.

BANK.q: A client on scheduled oxycodone for 3 days has not had a bowel movement. The nurse explains this is because opioids:
BANK.r: Opioid receptors are in the GI tract; activation decreases GI motility → constipation. Other effects: euphoria/addiction, hypotension, respiratory depression, sedation.

BANK.q: During the inflammatory response, what causes redness and warmth at an injury?
BANK.r: Vasodilation → redness and warmth. Increased capillary permeability → swelling/edema. Sensitized nerve endings → pain.

BANK.q: A client asks how much acetaminophen is safe per day. Using the course limit, the nurse answers:
BANK.r: Supplied maximum daily dose: 4,000 mg. Main danger: hepatotoxicity; alcohol increases liver risk.

BANK.q: A client takes acetaminophen all day and drinks wine nightly. What is the priority concern?
BANK.r: Acetaminophen → liver damage at high doses; alcohol increases liver risk.

BANK.q: A client taking daily aspirin reports black, tarry stools. The nurse recognizes this as:
o: A sign of GI bleeding from COX-1 inhibition
BANK.r: COX-1 inhibitors (aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen) remove gastric protection and decrease platelet aggregation → GI ulcer and bleeding.

BANK.q: Which medication is a COX-2 inhibitor?
BANK.r: COX-2: celecoxib, valdecoxib. COX-1: aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen.

BANK.q: Which effects are expected when an opioid agonist activates mu receptors? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Dampened CNS → sedation; decreased vascular resistance → hypotension; decreased GI motility → constipation; pleasure → addiction potential.

BANK.q: Which statement about opioid agonists and antagonists is correct?
o: An antagonist binds a receptor to cause a response
An agonist binds a receptor to block a response
Naloxone binds receptors to block or reverse a response
BANK.r: Agonist binds → causes a response (morphine, fentanyl, hydromorphone). Antagonist binds → blocks/reverses (naloxone).

BANK.q: A client on prednisone for months says, "I feel great, so I'm stopping it today." Best response?
o: "The dose has to be tapered slowly; stopping suddenly can cause adrenal crisis."
"Cut the dose in half tomorrow and stop."
BANK.r: Endogenous glucocorticoids are suppressed; abrupt withdrawal → adrenal crisis. Taper slowly.

BANK.q: Glucocorticoids decrease edema primarily because they:
BANK.r: Glucocorticoids mimic cortisol, prevent release of leukotrienes, prostaglandins, histamine, and decrease capillary permeability → less pain, inflammation, edema.

BANK.q: Gout most commonly causes pain, swelling and redness in which joint?
BANK.r: Gout = uric acid crystals deposit in joint spaces, especially the big toe.

BANK.q: How do antihyperuricemics such as allopurinol work?
BANK.r: They decrease uric acid by decreasing resorption or increasing kidney excretion → renal-stone risk → hydrate.

BANK.q: Which chemicals does the brain release as the body's natural painkillers?
BANK.r: Natural painkillers: serotonin, enkephalins, endorphins — often not enough for severe or chronic pain.

BANK.q: Tramadol is a dual-mechanism analgesic. Compared with morphine, respiratory-center suppression with tramadol is described as:
BANK.r: Tramadol activates opioid receptors; suppression of brainstem respiratory centers is described as rare.

BANK.q: Which client statement is most consistent with restless legs syndrome?
o: "My legs feel better when I lie still."
"The crawling feeling goes away when I get up and walk."
"I suddenly fall asleep when I laugh."
"My partner says I snore and stop breathing."
BANK.r: RLS: unpleasant leg sensations + urge to move, at rest (usually bedtime), relieved by movement.

BANK.q: Which can trigger or contribute to restless legs syndrome? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: RLS risks: insufficient sleep, pregnancy, iron deficiency, MS, dopamine abnormalities; antidepressants, metoclopramide, haloperidol.

BANK.q: A client on warfarin is prescribed ropinirole (Requip). Which lab does the nurse monitor closely?
BANK.r: Ropinirole may interact with warfarin and raise INR. Also: drowsiness, dizziness, syncope, falls.

BANK.q: Which statement shows correct understanding of zolpidem (Ambien)?
o: "I'll take it after dinner so it kicks in by bedtime."
"I'll take it right before getting into bed when I can sleep at least 7 hours."
"A glass of wine with it will help me relax."
"I can add another sleep aid if it doesn't work."
BANK.r: Take immediately before bed (rapid onset), plan ≥7 hours sleep, never with alcohol or other sleep meds.

BANK.q: A client on zolpidem reports his wife found him cooking at 2 AM with no memory of it. Best action?
o: Notify the provider; the medication should be discontinued
Teach him to lock the kitchen
BANK.r: Boxed warning: complex sleep behaviors. Alert provider and discontinue immediately — don't just monitor.

BANK.q: A 19-year-old collapses to her knees from sudden loss of muscle tone whenever she laughs hard. This is:
BANK.r: Cataplexy = emotion-triggered loss of muscle tone, seen with narcolepsy (onset 15–30).

BANK.q: Which medication is first-line for narcolepsy?
BANK.r: First-line: modafinil or armodafinil (non-amphetamine wake-promoting). Methylphenidate used rarely (addiction).

BANK.q: A client with heart failure who takes opioids has witnessed breathing pauses at night but does NOT snore. Suspected condition?
BANK.r: CSA: airway open but brain fails to signal breathing. Risks: opioids, HF, stroke. Apnea without snoring.

BANK.q: Which are risk factors for obstructive sleep apnea? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: OSA risks: obesity, older age, male, neck >17 in, smoking/alcohol, airway abnormalities, supine sleep. Side-sleeping treats mild OSA.

BANK.q: Which test can distinguish obstructive from central sleep apnea?
BANK.r: PSG = in-lab gold standard; distinguishes OSA vs CSA. HSAT is cheaper but cannot.

BANK.q: A 6-year-old with enlarged tonsils has obstructive sleep apnea. First-line treatment?
BANK.r: Pediatric OSA first-line = adenotonsillectomy. Adult first-line = CPAP.

BANK.q: Which melatonin teaching is correct?
o: Start with 1 mg about 30 minutes before bed
It is habit-forming; limit to 1 week
Take with alcohol for a stronger effect
BANK.r: OTC, non-habit-forming. 30 min before bed; start 1 mg, titrate up.

BANK.q: A client with hypoventilation-type central sleep apnea needs positive airway pressure. Preferred device?
BANK.r: Hyperventilation CSA → CPAP. Hypoventilation CSA → BiPAP (two pressures).

BANK.q: Which sleep-hygiene teaching is appropriate for insomnia? Select all that apply.
o: Keep consistent bed and wake times
Keep the room quiet, dark and cool
Limit caffeine later in the day
BANK.r: Exercise during the day but NOT right before bed. Also CBT-I, relaxation, meditation.

BANK.q: A client with OSA stopped using CPAP because the mask is uncomfortable. Best nursing response?
o: Explore mask type/fit changes, humidification and gradual acclimation
Switch to oxygen by nasal cannula
BANK.r: CPAP is first-line but adherence is poor (mask discomfort, noise). Troubleshoot fit, humidification, gradual acclimation.

BANK.q: A client with poorly controlled hypertension reports new morning headaches and daytime sleepiness. What should the nurse ask about?
BANK.r: OSA links: hypertension, CVD, diabetes. Day findings: morning headache, sleepiness, irritability. Ask about snoring/witnessed apnea.

BANK.q: Which non-drug measures help restless legs syndrome? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Non-pharm RLS: avoid alcohol/nicotine/caffeine, regular sleep, moderate exercise, massage, warm baths, heat/ice, stretching.

BANK.q: Ropinirole (Requip) is used for RLS because it:
BANK.r: Ropinirole = dopamine agonist, taken at night. RLS linked to impaired dopamine transmission in the basal ganglia.

BANK.q: Before starting RLS treatment, which labs does the nurse expect to be checked?
BANK.r: Iron deficiency is an RLS risk factor: check iron and ferritin; replace with ferrous sulfate PO or IV.

BANK.q: A client is prescribed Intermezzo (low-dose sublingual zolpidem) for middle-of-the-night waking. When may it be taken?
o: Only with 4 or more hours of sleep remaining
BANK.r: Intermezzo: only if ≥4 hours of sleep remain. Standard Ambien: plan ≥7 hours.

BANK.q: Which action best promotes sleep for a hospitalized client?
o: Wake the client hourly for vital signs
Cluster care and reduce nighttime noise and light
Keep the overhead light on for safety
BANK.r: Hospitalized: cluster care, manage noise/light, reduce interruptions, ask to move nonessential overnight med times.

BANK.q: What is the hallmark finding of narcolepsy?
o: Excessive daytime drowsiness with sudden sleep attacks
BANK.r: Narcolepsy: extreme daytime drowsiness + involuntary sleep attacks lasting seconds–minutes regardless of prior sleep.

BANK.q: Which teaching is appropriate for a client with narcolepsy?
o: Take regularly scheduled naps and keep a sleep schedule
BANK.r: Keep a sleep schedule, scheduled naps, avoid alcohol/nicotine, exercise regularly.

BANK.q: Which is an advantage of home sleep apnea testing (HSAT) over polysomnography?
BANK.r: HSAT: portable, convenient, cheaper, slightly less accurate, cannot distinguish OSA vs CSA.

BANK.q: After a child's adenotonsillectomy for OSA, snoring is gone. What does the nurse reinforce?
o: Follow-up sleep study to confirm resolution
BANK.r: Do not assume improvement means cure — reinforce a follow-up sleep study.

BANK.q: Which statement about CPAP vs BiPAP is correct?
o: BiPAP gives separate inhalation and exhalation pressures
BANK.r: CPAP: one continuous pressure, 4–20, portable. BiPAP: two pressures, 4–30, more expensive.

BANK.q: Which explains why central sleep apnea usually has no snoring?
o: The airway is open; the brain fails to send the signal to breathe
BANK.r: CSA: no obstruction, so nothing vibrates. Pauses in effort; Cheyne-Stokes-like pattern.

BANK.q: What is first-line treatment for adult OSA regardless of severity?
BANK.r: CPAP is first-line regardless of severity. Surgery is secondary if CPAP not tolerated.

BANK.q: Why might melatonin be preferred over zolpidem for an older hospitalized adult?
o: It is a Schedule IV drug
Less confusion and fall risk; non-habit forming
BANK.r: Melatonin: cost-effective, non-habit forming, lower confusion/fall risk in older adults.

BANK.q: A client receiving external beam radiation asks if he is radioactive. Correct response?
o: "No. You and your body fluids are not radioactive. Don't wash off the markings."
"Only your urine is radioactive for 48 hours."
BANK.r: External beam: not radioactive; keep tattoo markings. Expect dermatitis, fatigue, marrow suppression.

BANK.q: A client has an intracavitary radiation implant. Which nursing action is correct?
o: Assign a pregnant nurse since exposure is minimal
Keep long-handled forceps and a lead container in the room
Spend extra time at the bedside
BANK.r: Radioactive until removed: private room, door closed, lead apron, ~1 hr/day exposure, no pregnant staff/visitors, forceps + lead container.

BANK.q: A client received chemotherapy 8 days ago. What is expected now?
BANK.r: Nadir: lowest counts 7–10 days after chemo; recovery another 5–7 days.

BANK.q: A client is at risk for tumor lysis syndrome. Which lab changes are expected? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Dying cells spill contents: HIGH K, uric acid, phosphorus; LOW calcium → dysrhythmias, seizures, renal failure.

BANK.q: A client with metastatic breast cancer has new back pain that is worse lying down. Priority?
o: Heating pad and reassess in 4 hours
Notify the provider promptly — suspect spinal cord compression
BANK.r: SCC red flag. Intervene within 24 hours to prevent paralysis. MRI = gold standard.

BANK.q: A client on chemo has oral temp 101.4°F and ANC 400/mm³. What comes first?
o: Two blood-culture sets from different sites before the first antibiotic
BANK.r: Neutropenic fever: ≥101°F + ANC <500 → 2 culture sets, then prompt antibiotics. No rectal temps, no fresh fruit/flowers.

BANK.q: A client with small-cell lung cancer has sodium 116 mEq/L. Priority intervention?
BANK.r: SIADH: excess ADH → water retention → dilutional hyponatremia; ~110 → seizures. Fluid restriction, I&O, daily weights.

BANK.q: Which are CAUTION warning signs of cancer? Select all that apply.
o: A sore that does not heal
Change in bowel or bladder habits
Obvious change in a wart or mole
BANK.r: C-bowel/bladder change, A-sore that won't heal, U-unusual bleeding, T-thickening/lump, I-indigestion/swallowing, O-wart/mole change, N-nagging cough.

BANK.q: A Pap test shows cells with abnormal structure that may be precancerous. Term?
BANK.r: Dysplasia = abnormal structure, may be precancerous. Hyperplasia = more NORMAL cells.

BANK.q: In which stage of carcinogenesis does a tumor develop its own blood supply?
BANK.r: Initiation (DNA altered) → Promotion (growth stimulated) → Progression (angiogenesis/VEGF) → Metastasis.

BANK.q: A client with lung cancer has edema of the face, neck and arms and dyspnea at rest. Appropriate action?
o: Elevate the head of the bed
BANK.r: SVC syndrome: monitor ABCs, elevate HOB, rest, strict I&O, avoid fluid overload.

BANK.q: Platelets are 40,000/µL after chemotherapy. Which instruction is correct?
o: Use an electric razor and soft toothbrush
BANK.r: Thrombocytopenia: bleeding precautions — electric razor, soft toothbrush, avoid straining/contact sports.

BANK.q: Chemotherapy given BEFORE surgery to shrink a tumor is called:
BANK.r: Neoadjuvant = before surgery. Adjuvant = after surgery.

BANK.q: Per the lecture, average-risk colonoscopy screening begins at:
BANK.r: Colonoscopy 45 q10y; mammogram yearly at 40; Pap q3y from 21; PSA/DRE ~50; low-dose CT for smokers ~50.

BANK.q: Which characteristics describe MALIGNANT cells? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Malignant: irregular, not encapsulated, large nucleus, loose adherence, migrates, aneuploid. Benign: encapsulated, tight, no metastasis.

BANK.q: In TNM staging, what does the 'N' describe?
BANK.r: T = primary tumor size/extent, N = regional nodes, M = distant metastasis. Higher numbers = more concerning.

BANK.q: For how long after chemotherapy does the nurse use body-fluid precautions, as taught?
BANK.r: Body-fluid precautions 48 hours after chemo. Only trained staff handle chemo, with PPE.

BANK.q: A client with multiple myeloma has calcium 12 mg/dL, confusion and constipation. Which order is expected first?
BANK.r: Hypercalcemia ≥10.6: rapid rehydration → furosemide; bisphosphonates; calcitonin works fast but not alone (rebound).

BANK.q: A client with an advanced bowel tumor has surgery to relieve an obstruction and improve comfort. This surgery is:
BANK.r: Palliative: relieve obstruction, debulk, reduce pain, improve QOL. Prophylactic = remove high-risk tissue (BRCA mastectomy).

BANK.q: A client with chemotherapy-induced mucositis asks about mouth care. Correct teaching?
o: Frequent oral care, ice chips, and baking-soda rinses
Eat spicy foods to stimulate saliva
BANK.r: Mucositis: ice/ice pops, frequent oral care, avoid alcohol mouthwash, baking-soda rinse.

BANK.q: Which skin-care teaching is correct for a client receiving external radiation?
o: Scrub the area to remove markings
Mild soap; avoid friction and sun; only prescribed unscented lotion
BANK.r: Mild soap, avoid friction and sun, only prescribed unscented non-drying lotion; don't remove markings.

BANK.q: A client has permanent prostate seed implants. Which teaching is correct?
o: Avoid close contact with pregnant people while radiation dissipates
BANK.r: Interstitial seeds: low radiation dissipates over months; avoid pregnant people; urine/stool not radioactive.

BANK.q: A client is treated with radioactive iodine (systemic radiation) for thyroid cancer. Which is true?
o: Body fluids are radioactive; precautions about 7 days
BANK.r: Systemic radiation: patient and body fluids radioactive; precautions ~7 days as taught.

BANK.q: Which medication increases neutrophil counts after chemotherapy?
BANK.r: Neutrophils: filgrastim, pegfilgrastim. RBCs: epoetin alfa, darbepoetin. Dexrazoxane = cytoprotectant.

BANK.q: Which teaching is appropriate for a client with neutropenia? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid fresh flowers and fresh fruit
BANK.r: Neutropenic teaching: handwashing, avoid crowds/sick people/fresh fruit/flowers, report fever. Oral or axillary temps only.

BANK.q: Which medication is used to manage hyperuricemia in tumor lysis syndrome?
BANK.r: TLS: telemetry, IV hydration, renal diet low in K/phos, allopurinol; rasburicase with kidney impairment; dialysis if needed.

BANK.q: What is the gold-standard test for suspected spinal cord compression?
BANK.r: MRI = gold standard. Treat with surgery, radiation or steroids; frequent neuro checks.

BANK.q: In SIADH, why is sodium low?
o: Excess ADH causes water retention that dilutes sodium
The kidneys excrete too much water
BANK.r: Excess ADH → water retention, can't excrete dilute urine → dilutional hyponatremia.

BANK.q: Which nursing teaching applies to a client with cancer-related hypercalcemia?
o: Drink 3–4 quarts/day if allowed, high-fiber diet, ambulate if safe
BANK.r: Encourage 3–4 qt/day oral fluids (sodium-containing), I&O, high fiber, ambulate, fall precautions, avoid calcium vitamins/antacids.

BANK.q: Gingival overgrowth from phenytoin (Dilantin) is an example of:
BANK.r: Hyperplasia = increased number of normal cells in response to a stimulus (phenytoin gingival hyperplasia, BPH).

BANK.q: In which stage does a carcinogen alter cellular DNA?
BANK.r: Initiation = carcinogen alters DNA. Promotion = hormones/proteins stimulate growth.

BANK.q: Which is an example of PRIMARY cancer prevention?
BANK.r: Primary = prevent it starting (no smoking, HPV vaccine, diet, UV avoidance). Secondary = screening/early detection.

BANK.q: Why is a port or central line used for chemotherapy?
BANK.r: A port/central line helps reduce extravasation injury.

BANK.q: A client fears infertility from chemotherapy. What should the nurse discuss BEFORE treatment?
BANK.r: Fertility changes: offer sperm or egg banking before treatment.

BANK.q: What is the most common cause of superior vena cava syndrome?
BANK.r: SVC syndrome: tumor compresses the SVC; lung cancer most common cause.

BANK.q: Which describes a benign tumor?
o: Clear borders, often encapsulated, no metastasis
BANK.r: Benign: clear borders, encapsulated, tight adherence, euploid, no metastasis.

BANK.q: In the CAUTION mnemonic, what does the 'I' stand for?
BANK.r: I = indigestion or difficulty swallowing.

BANK.q: The monitor shows ventricular tachycardia. FIRST action?
o: Go to the patient and check for a pulse
BANK.r: The pulse decides the path. No pulse → CPR + defib; pulse + unstable → sync cardioversion; pulse + stable → amiodarone/lidocaine.

BANK.q: Right after adenosine IV push, the monitor shows a 5-second pause. What does the nurse do?
o: Recognize this as expected and keep monitoring
BANK.r: Brief asystole after adenosine is expected. Warn the patient beforehand (flushing, chest pressure, impending doom).

BANK.q: Which technique is correct for adenosine?
o: Slow push over 2 minutes, distal port
Rapid push at the closest port, then 20 mL NS flush and elevate the arm
BANK.r: Half-life <10 s: rapid push, closest port, immediate 20 mL flush, elevate extremity.

BANK.q: A client in SVT at 210 bpm has BP 74/40 and is confused. Anticipated intervention?
BANK.r: Unstable SVT → synchronized cardioversion. Stable → vagal → adenosine → BB/CCB.

BANK.q: A client with a prolonged QT develops polymorphic VT twisting around the baseline, with a pulse. First-line drug?
BANK.r: Torsades = twisting + long QT + magnesium (even if Mg is normal).

BANK.q: During a magnesium infusion, which finding is the earliest sign of toxicity?
BANK.r: Earliest toxicity: decreased DTRs → notify. Flushing is expected. Antidote: calcium gluconate.

BANK.q: A client is pulseless with asystole confirmed in two leads. Correct treatment?
BANK.r: Asystole is not shockable — no chaos to clear. CPR + epinephrine + reversible causes.

BANK.q: The monitor shows a normal-looking rhythm, but the client is unresponsive with no pulse. This is:
BANK.r: PEA: organized rhythm, no pulse. Can't diagnose from the monitor alone. CPR + epi; no shock.

BANK.q: A client in third-degree heart block is dizzy, BP 78/42. Priority?
BANK.r: Atropine must not delay pacing. Pads, O2, IV, monitor, notify. Permanent pacemaker is definitive.

BANK.q: The nurse sees three consecutive PVCs. How is this documented?
BANK.r: Couplet = 2 in a row. ≥3 consecutive PVCs = VT.

BANK.q: The day after pacemaker insertion, the client has persistent hiccups. Best action?
o: Report it — the lead may be pacing the diaphragm
Have the client hold their breath
BANK.r: Persistent hiccups → lead may have shifted and be pacing the diaphragm. Report.

BANK.q: Which discharge teaching is correct for a new permanent pacemaker? Select all that apply.
o: Don't raise the affected arm above the shoulder for 2–3 weeks
Call if pulse is below the set rate
No lifting more than 10–15 lb for 2–3 weeks
BANK.r: Microwaves/household appliances are safe. Avoid strong magnets over the generator. Know the set rate.

BANK.q: During synchronized cardioversion, which action requires the nurse to intervene?
o: Leaving oxygen flowing at the bedside during the shock
BANK.r: No oxygen during the shock (fire risk); apply after. SYNC avoids shocking on the T wave.

BANK.q: A pacer spike followed by a QRS is on the monitor. How does the nurse confirm mechanical capture?
o: Palpate a pulse that matches the paced complexes
BANK.r: Electrical capture = spike + complex. Mechanical capture = palpable pulse.

BANK.q: Which second-degree AV block is more dangerous and can progress abruptly to complete heart block?
BANK.r: Mobitz II: dropped QRS with constant PR. Anticipate pacing; atropine often ineffective. Wenckebach: longer, longer, drop.

BANK.q: Which side effect is expected after atropine for symptomatic bradycardia?
BANK.r: Anticholinergic: tachycardia, dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, confusion (older adults). Caution after MI.

BANK.q: A post-MI client develops frequent multifocal PVCs. Which labs does the nurse check?
BANK.r: PVC causes: low K/Mg, hypoxia/ischemia, stimulants, digoxin toxicity. Multifocal/frequent post-MI → notify.

BANK.q: A client with stable SVT at 180 bpm. What is tried first?
BANK.r: Stable SVT: vagal maneuvers → adenosine → BB/CCB; ablation if recurrent.

BANK.q: Which can trigger SVT? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Triggers: stress, fatigue, caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, stimulants (pseudoephedrine), ischemia, low Mg/K, hyperthyroid.

BANK.q: Adenosine is contraindicated in which client?
BANK.r: Contraindicated in 2nd/3rd-degree AV block; caution with asthma.

BANK.q: Why must the SYNC button be on for cardioversion?
o: Prevents shocking on the T wave, which can cause V-fib
BANK.r: Synchronization avoids the vulnerable T wave. Defibrillation (unsynchronized) is for pulseless rhythms.

BANK.q: Before cardioversion for atrial fibrillation, what must the nurse verify?
BANK.r: Before: consent, verify anticoagulation with AFib, baseline rhythm, emergency equipment.

BANK.q: A client in VT has a pulse, BP 118/72, and is alert. Expected treatment?
o: IV amiodarone or lidocaine and correct K/Mg
BANK.r: Stable VT with pulse: amiodarone/lidocaine, correct K/Mg, 12-lead, prepare for cardioversion.

BANK.q: A client is in V-fib. Which treatment is correct?
BANK.r: V-fib: no cardiac output; shockable. CPR + unsynchronized defibrillation.

BANK.q: Torsades de pointes becomes pulseless. Correct shock?
BANK.r: The varying complexes can't be synchronized → unsynchronized defibrillation.

BANK.q: Which is the antidote for magnesium toxicity?
BANK.r: Calcium gluconate. Mg is diluted and run on a pump — never gravity or routine IV push.

BANK.q: Which describes first-degree AV block?
o: PR > 0.20 sec and constant; every P followed by QRS
No relationship between P and QRS
BANK.r: Delayed, not blocked: PR >0.20 constant. Usually benign; monitor for progression.

BANK.q: Which finding describes third-degree heart block?
o: P waves and QRS complexes march independently
BANK.r: Complete AV dissociation: P waves at one rate, QRS at a slower rate, PR varies.

BANK.q: Why is atropine used cautiously after an acute MI?
o: Increasing HR increases myocardial oxygen demand
BANK.r: Atropine raises HR → higher O2 demand.

BANK.q: Most patients have a demand pacemaker. What does it do?
o: Fires regardless of the heart's rhythm
Fires only when the intrinsic rate drops below the set rate
BANK.r: Demand mode senses beats and fires only below the programmed rate. Fixed rate fires regardless.

BANK.q: Which test confirms pacemaker lead placement and checks for pneumothorax?
BANK.r: Chest X-ray confirms lead placement and checks for pneumothorax/hemothorax.

BANK.q: A healthy, asymptomatic client has an occasional isolated PVC. Usual management?
BANK.r: Isolated PVCs in a healthy asymptomatic patient are generally not treated.

BANK.q: How does VT reduce cardiac output?
o: Fast rate reduces filling time plus uncoordinated contraction
BANK.r: Poor filling + poor ejection → rapid loss of cardiac output.

BANK.q: A DEXA T-score is -2.0. Interpretation?
BANK.r: 0 to -1 normal; -1 to -2.5 osteopenia; below -2.5 osteoporosis.

BANK.q: Which statement shows understanding of alendronate?
o: "First thing in the morning with a full glass of water, then stay upright 30 minutes."
BANK.r: Empty stomach ~30 min before eating, 8 oz water, upright 30 min (esophagitis). Not for GERD.

BANK.q: Before starting calcitonin nasal spray, what is most important to ask?
BANK.r: Salmon derivative. One spray daily, alternate nostrils, continue Ca + vit D.

BANK.q: Which cells build bone?
BANK.r: OsteoBlasts = Building; osteoclasts = resorption.

BANK.q: Which increase osteoporosis risk? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: PPIs/steroids/anticonvulsants increase Ca excretion; smoking, alcohol, caffeine, soda impair absorption; kidney disease ↑ phosphorus.

BANK.q: Which is one of the earliest signs of osteoporosis?
BANK.r: Loss of height (2–3 in) — spongy bone in the spine is affected first.

BANK.q: After vertebroplasty, the client has a headache and a ring of clear fluid around a center spot on the dressing. Suspect:
BANK.r: Halo/bullseye sign + headache → CSF leak. Post-op priority: neurovascular assessment.

BANK.q: Highest-priority intervention for a client with osteoporosis at home?
o: Remove scatter rugs and ensure good lighting
BANK.r: Fall prevention is of utmost importance; most injuries happen at home.

BANK.q: How does kyphoplasty differ from vertebroplasty?
BANK.r: Vertebroplasty = cement (recent). Kyphoplasty = balloon + cement (older, >3 months).

BANK.q: What does PTH do when serum calcium is low?
o: Pulls calcium from bone into blood
BANK.r: PTH pulls Ca FROM bone. Calcitonin keeps Ca IN bone.

BANK.q: Which exercise is recommended for osteoporosis?
BANK.r: Weight-bearing: walking, biking, weight training — 30 min 3x/week.

BANK.q: Which beverage interferes with calcium absorption?
BANK.r: Tannins/oxalic acid in tea, iced tea and coffee interfere. Fat also reduces calcium access.

BANK.q: Before vertebroplasty, which medication history is most important?
o: Blood thinners — usually stopped 5–7 days before
BANK.r: Pre-procedure: NPO, nurse validates consent, screen for blood thinners (stop ~5–7 days).

BANK.q: Which osteoporosis drug class carries an emphasized clot risk?
BANK.r: SERMs mimic estrogen: increase bone density, reduce resorption — clot risk emphasized.

BANK.q: What is the gold-standard screening test for osteoporosis?
BANK.r: DEXA: noninvasive, painless, very low radiation; compares to peak bone mass ~age 30. X-ray misses until ~25% loss.

BANK.q: A T-score of -2.8 indicates:
BANK.r: Below -2.5 = osteoporosis.

BANK.q: Per lecture, routine osteoporosis screening is recommended for:
BANK.r: Women >65, men >70; special-risk screening may begin ~50.

BANK.q: A client on ibandronate reports loose teeth and exposed jawbone. The nurse suspects:
BANK.r: Rare bisphosphonate adverse effect: osteonecrosis of the jaw.

BANK.q: Correct calcitonin nasal spray technique?
o: One spray daily, alternating nostrils, at room temperature
BANK.r: One spray/day, alternate nostrils, stored in fridge but used at room temp.

BANK.q: After about age 30, what happens to bone?
BANK.r: Growth and removal balance until ~30; after that resorption increases. Peak bone mass built ~25–35.

BANK.q: A client with kidney disease has high phosphorus. Effect on bone?
o: Calcium falls, body pulls calcium from bone
BANK.r: Phosphorus ↑ → calcium ↓ → calcium pulled from bone.

BANK.q: Osteoporosis usually begins in which type of bone?
o: Spongy (cancellous) bone — spine, ribs, pelvis, wrist
BANK.r: Spongy bone first; honeycomb appearance as resorption exceeds formation.

BANK.q: Which factor reduces vitamin D synthesis from sunlight?
BANK.r: Interfering: sunscreen, cloudy/rainy regions, dark skin pigment. Lecture: ~800–1,000 IU.

BANK.q: A client takes extra calcium supplements thinking 'more is better'. Which effect can over-supplementation cause?
BANK.r: Over-supplementation: constipation, kidney stones, reduced iron/zinc absorption, bradycardia/cardiac arrest.

BANK.q: Which medication class builds bone by stimulating osteoblasts?
BANK.r: PTH analogs stimulate osteoblasts. Bisphosphonates/RANKL inhibitors block breakdown.

BANK.q: Denosumab (RANKL inhibitor) is given how?
BANK.r: RANKL inhibitors block osteoclasts; denosumab SQ every 6 months.

BANK.q: First approach for a new vertebral compression fracture?
o: Conservative: rest, pain management, temporary bracing
BANK.r: Conservative first; vertebroplasty/kyphoplasty if it fails.

BANK.q: Which medication increases fall risk in a client with osteoporosis?
BANK.r: Review antihypertensives (orthostasis) and sedating medications.

BANK.q: Why does weight-bearing exercise help bone?
o: Muscle contraction against bone keeps calcium in bone
BANK.r: Muscle pull on bone increases density and keeps calcium in bone.

BANK.q: Which finding is consistent with osteoarthritis?
o: Stiffness after inactivity, crepitus, Heberden's nodes
All-day morning stiffness with symmetric joints
BANK.r: OA is local: stiffness with disuse, crepitus, osteophytes (Heberden's distal, Bouchard's proximal). RA is systemic.

BANK.q: Which exercise is probably best for OA per the professor?
BANK.r: Swimming: resistance strengthens muscles, low impact.

BANK.q: Correct teaching for a lidocaine patch for knee OA?
BANK.r: Lidocaine patch: 12 on, 12 off.

BANK.q: After posterior-approach total hip replacement, which action requires intervention?
BANK.r: No crossing legs, no flexion >90°, keep abducted.

BANK.q: After THR the client feels a 'pop'; the leg is shorter and externally rotated. Priority?
o: Keep in bed and notify the surgeon immediately
BANK.r: Signs of dislocation → keep in bed, notify surgeon.

BANK.q: Main concern after total knee replacement?
BANK.r: Knee: prevent contracture; progressive ROM with bending and full extension; ice first 24 hr; immobilizer initially.

BANK.q: Pre-op urinalysis for TKR shows a UTI. What should happen?
o: Treat and clear the infection before surgery
BANK.r: No infection anywhere before joint replacement (prosthetic failure). Clear ~2–4 weeks before.

BANK.q: Which test best evaluates cartilage health in OA?
BANK.r: X-ray: narrowing/osteophytes. MRI: cartilage. No single lab diagnoses OA.

BANK.q: Before ambulating a joint-replacement client on post-op day 1, the nurse must know:
BANK.r: Know weight-bearing order first. Press-fit may need NWB/toe-touch until bone grows in.

BANK.q: Primary pain-relief choice for OA in lecture, and its max daily dose?
BANK.r: Acetaminophen, max 4 g/day. Opioids if others fail: start low, go slow.

BANK.q: Which are OA risk factors? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Age >60, obesity, repetitive use, WOMEN, smoking, genetics.

BANK.q: What is the correct order of OA joint changes?
o: Cartilage softens/thins → joint space narrows → bone-on-bone → osteophytes
BANK.r: Cartilage degenerates → narrowing → bone rubs bone → thickens and forms osteophytes.

BANK.q: When is joint replacement indicated for OA?
o: Severe pain and loss of function
BANK.r: Severe pain + loss of function/inadequate pain control → arthroplasty.

BANK.q: Which post-op joint-replacement interventions prevent DVT? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: DVT prevention: SCDs + anticoagulant + early ambulation; DVT/PE peaks up to 2 weeks; prophylaxis ~1 month.

BANK.q: Bouchard's nodes are found at which joint?
BANK.r: Heberden's = distal; Bouchard's = proximal.

BANK.q: Where does OA most commonly occur?
BANK.r: Commonly weight-bearing joints: hips, knees, spine.

BANK.q: A client on long-term NSAIDs for OA may also be prescribed:
BANK.r: NSAIDs → GI upset/bleeding; PPI with long-term use.

BANK.q: About how often can cortisone be injected into an OA joint, per the professor?
BANK.r: Cortisone injection limited (~4x/year). Hyaluronic acid/Synvisc ~2x/year.

BANK.q: A client starting cyclobenzaprine for OA muscle spasm should be taught:
BANK.r: Muscle relaxants (cyclobenzaprine, diazepam): sleepiness can occur.

BANK.q: Which adaptive device would OT provide for a client with OA hands?
BANK.r: Large-handled utensils, long-handled grippers, shoehorns, large buttons, Velcro.

BANK.q: Before PT exercises for a client with OA, the nurse should:
BANK.r: Adequate pain control is needed for participation in PT/OT.

BANK.q: What is the fundamental feature of osteoarthritis?
BANK.r: OA = degeneration of joint cartilage; chronic, progressive — manage, not cure.

BANK.q: Why does weight loss help OA?
o: Decreases joint stress and pain and slows degeneration
BANK.r: Obesity stresses joints; weight control reduces pain and slows degeneration.

BANK.q: Why might rheumatoid factor be drawn in suspected OA?
BANK.r: No single lab diagnoses OA; RF rules out RA. ESR/CRP reflect inflammation.

BANK.q: Which pre-op teaching applies before joint replacement? Select all that apply.
BANK.r: Pre-op: cough/deep breathe, IS, SCDs, expect pain control; antibiotic within 1 hr of incision.

BANK.q: Which assessment is a post-op joint-replacement priority?
BANK.r: Priorities: respiratory and neurovascular (6 Ps: pain, pallor, pulses, paresthesia, paralysis, pressure).

BANK.q: Which instruction prevents hip dislocation after THR?
BANK.r: No flexion >90°, no crossing, abduction pillow, raised toilet seat.

BANK.q: What is commonly used in the first 24 hours after TKR?
BANK.r: Ice packs first 24 hr; knee immobilizer may maintain extension; gradual ROM.

BANK.q: A press-fitted (uncemented) hip may initially require:
o: Non-weight-bearing or toe-touch until bone grows in
BANK.r: Press-fit is porous; bone grows in ~3 months. Cemented hips often tolerate PWB/FWB.

BANK.q: About what percent of hip replacements result from OA rather than fracture, per lecture?
BANK.r: About 70% of hip replacements are from osteoarthritis.

BANK.q: A client with a casted tibial fracture has pain unrelieved by morphine that worsens with passive toe stretch. Suspect:
BANK.r: ACS early: pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, paresthesia, tense compartment → fasciotomy.

BANK.q: For suspected compartment syndrome, how is the extremity positioned?
BANK.r: Remove restrictions, heart level only, 5 Ps q15min, notify, prepare for fasciotomy.

BANK.q: 24 hours after a femur fracture, the client is confused, short of breath, with chest petechiae. Priority?
BANK.r: Fat embolism (12–48 hr): lungs + brain + petechiae. ABCs, O2, ABGs.

BANK.q: A crush victim has tea-colored urine and very high CK. Expected order?
o: Aggressive isotonic IV fluids, UO ~200–300 mL/hr
BANK.r: Rhabdo: myoglobin → AKI. Aggressive IV fluids, strict I&O, ECG (high K).

BANK.q: Which shows correct crutch use on stairs?
o: Up with the bad, down with the good
Up with the good, down with the bad
BANK.r: Up with the good, down with the bad.

BANK.q: Traction weights are resting on the floor. What should be done?
BANK.r: Weights hang freely, ropes in pulleys, alignment maintained.

BANK.q: Which cast-care instructions are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Keep dry with a waterproof protector
Scratch under it with a hanger
BANK.r: Dry + elevate + nothing inside. Report 5-P changes, odor, tightness.

BANK.q: A 2-year-old has a spiral femur fracture. Priority consideration?
BANK.r: Spiral = twisting; in children assess for abuse.

BANK.q: An overstretched ankle LIGAMENT is a:
BANK.r: Sprain = ligament (bone-bone). Strain = muscle/tendon.

BANK.q: Which prevents hip flexion contracture after an above-knee amputation?
o: Residual limb on a pillow at all times
Sit in a recliner all day
BANK.r: Prone q3–4h for 20–30 min, alignment, firm mattress; elevate residual limb initially only.

BANK.q: Backs of hands together, wrists flexed for 60 seconds → tingling. Which test?
BANK.r: Phalen = wrist flexion; Tinel = tapping median nerve.

BANK.q: Which of the 5 Ps is an EARLY warning sign?
BANK.r: Paresthesia early; pulselessness/paralysis late.

BANK.q: Which fracture carries the highest infection risk?
BANK.r: Open: bone penetrates skin.

BANK.q: Which pain scale fits a nonverbal, cognitively impaired adult with a hip fracture?
BANK.r: FLACC (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability) for nonverbal/impaired or young children; Wong-Baker for kids who can point.

BANK.q: Which labs indicate muscle destruction?
BANK.r: CK + myoglobin = muscle destruction (rhabdo). ALP = bone healing; CRP/ESR = inflammation.

BANK.q: Which is the first stage of bone healing?
BANK.r: Hematoma → granulation → callus (3–6 wk) → true bone → consolidation/remodeling (up to 1 yr).

BANK.q: Day 4 after external fixation, a pin site has increasing purulent drainage and odor. Interpretation?
BANK.r: Clear drainage in first 48–72 hr can be normal; worsening drainage, odor, redness → infection (osteomyelitis/MRSA).

BANK.q: After amputation, the client reports burning in the missing foot. Which medication may help?
BANK.r: Phantom limb pain: burning, cramping, tingling; neuropathic/antiepileptic meds.

BANK.q: A toddler was lifted by the arm and now holds it stiff and refuses to use it. Likely:
BANK.r: Nursemaid elbow: radial-head subluxation after a sudden pull.

BANK.q: List the 5 Ps in order:
BANK.r: Pain → pallor/poikilothermia → paresthesia → pulselessness → paralysis.

BANK.q: Which is a LATE sign of compartment syndrome?
BANK.r: Late: pulselessness, paralysis, coolness, necrosis.

BANK.q: Fat embolism syndrome typically appears how long after a long-bone fracture?
BANK.r: FES 12–48 hr. Petechiae often appear last.

BANK.q: What is the major danger of rhabdomyolysis?
BANK.r: Myoglobin → AKI. Also high K → dysrhythmias.

BANK.q: Where should crutch pads sit?
o: About 1.5–2 inches (2–3 fingers) below the axilla
BANK.r: Weight through the hands; elbows ~30°; crutches 6 in to the side, 2 in in front.

BANK.q: How does skeletal traction differ from skin traction?
BANK.r: Skin: Velcro/boot, 5–10 lb. Skeletal: pins/tongs, 15–30 lb; pin-site care.

BANK.q: How long does a plaster cast take to dry?
BANK.r: Plaster ~24 hr, hot, absorbs drainage. Fiberglass dries quickly.

BANK.q: Why may a splint be used instead of a cast right after injury?
o: Allows swelling and reduces arterial occlusion risk
BANK.r: Splints allow swelling; may be removable for bathing.

BANK.q: POLICE stands for:
o: Protection, Optimal Loading, Ice, Compression, Elevation
Pain, Oxygen, Lift, Ice, Cast, Elevate
Position, Oral meds, Ice, Cast, Exercise
BANK.r: Ice 10–15 min every few hours; controlled weight-bearing as tolerated.

BANK.q: A greenstick fracture is:
o: A partial (incomplete) break common in children
BANK.r: Greenstick/incomplete: partial break, common in children. Comminuted = >3 fragments.

BANK.q: Post-amputation: BP 86/50, HR 128, H/H dropping. Suspect:
BANK.r: Hemorrhage/shock: hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, low H/H.

BANK.q: What is the first post-op priority after amputation?
BANK.r: ABCs/vitals first, then bleeding, infection, pain, contracture prevention, psychosocial support.

BANK.q: Which fingers are affected by carpal tunnel syndrome?
o: Thumb, index, middle and half of ring finger
BANK.r: Median nerve: thumb, index, middle, half ring; worse at night; thenar atrophy late.

BANK.q: Which test best shows the extent of soft-tissue damage?
BANK.r: X-ray: fracture; CT: complex (pelvis/spine); MRI: soft tissue.

BANK.q: How long does a healthy young adult's fracture typically take to heal?
BANK.r: Young adults ~4–6 weeks; older adults 2–3 months or longer.

BANK.q: How often are pin sites assessed after external fixation?
BANK.r: Pin sites q8–12h; monitor distal 5 Ps.

BANK.q: After giving an analgesic to a fracture client, pain is INCREASING. The nurse should suspect:
BANK.r: Reassess after analgesia; increasing pain may indicate compartment syndrome.
